newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HSBC 1996 results in line - analysts.
newsitem.headline: HSBC 1996 results in line - analysts.

text.p: International banking giant HSBC Holdings Plc's 1996 results were in line with expectations, but analysts were surprised by larger than expected provisions for problem loans at unit Hang Seng Bank Ltd.
"In terms of overall results there were no surprises," said Robin Hammond, Hong Kong research director at Asia Equity Ltd.
The banking group reported an attributable profit of HK$37.59 billion in 1996, a 25 percent growth over 1995. That was slightly better than the consensus estimate of a 24 percent increase.
Its 61.5 percent-held subsidiary Hang Seng Bank Ltd posted an attributable profit of HK$8.49 billion, a 6.3 percent rise over the previous year.
But its net charge for bad and doubtful debts grew to HK$715 million, compared with HK$131 million in 1995.
"Hang Seng's results were slightly disappointing," said Hammond, pointing to the marked increase in bad debt charges.

Said one analyst with a major regional brokerage:"At the operating profit level, the results were about four percent better than we had forecast...But bad debt provisions were about twice what we had expected."

The attributable profit of another HSBC unit, Midland Bank Plc of Britain, rose 39 percent to 849 million sterling due mainly to continued cost control and to a 3.0 percent rise in assets to 96.2 billion sterling, HSBC said.
The continued improvement in profitability at Midland pushed its contribution to total group earnings to 32 percent in 1996 from 31 percent in 1995, the parent said.
"Midland's results were positive, with better net interest income than expected," Hammond said.
The British unit's net interest income rose 7.55 percent to 2.05 billion sterling.
"Midland actually achieved asset growth," one analyst noted.
Analysts pointed out HSBC continues to lead the list of international banks in terms of capital backing.
"Tier one capital rose to 9.9 percent which is quite high," said the regional analyst. "If it keeps rising, it could affect the group's return on equity."
But one analyst with a U.S. brokerage firm said higher capital could mean better growth potential in the longer term.
"One can say that HSBC is conservative as regards capital management, but the higher the capital the faster you can grow," said one analyst with a U.S. brokerage firm.
Tier one capital is mainly shareholders' funds which include share capital, retained earnings and revaluation reserves.
The Bank of International Settlements has set a minimum requirement of 4.0 percent for Tier one capital.
